title: Homogeneous approximation at a projective point
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $r\geq0$, and $B=k[X_0,\ldots,X_r]$ with all variables of degree one [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. Let $\mathfrak p\subset k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ be a prime ideal, put $L=k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]_{\mathfrak p}$ and $N=\mathfrak pL$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], and define $\delta_d:B_d\to L$ by $\delta_d(\phi)=\phi(1,t_1,\ldots,t_r)/1$. Put $U_d=\{\phi\in B_d:\delta_d(\phi)\in N^d\}$. For $h\in L$ its order is $\sup\{n:h\in N^n\}$; for finite order $n$, its initial form is its class in $N^n/N^{n+1}\subset\operatorname{gr}_NL$ [def-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring]. Let $b\geq0$, $d\geq1$, and let nonzero forms $\phi_j\in U_{e_j}$ have degrees $1\leq e_j\leq d$ for $1\leq j\leq b$. Let $\psi\in B_d$ and let $t\geq1$. If there are $b_j\in L$ such that
$$\delta_d(\psi)-\sum_{j=1}^b b_j\delta_{e_j}(\phi_j)\in N^t,$$
then there are homogeneous $C_j\in B_{d-e_j}$ such that
$$\delta_d\left(\psi-\sum_{j=1}^b C_j\phi_j\right)\in N^t.$$
In particular, for $t=d$ the corrected form belongs to $U_d$; for $t>d$ one has $\psi\in(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_b)B$. Zero polynomials are allowed as homogeneous coefficients and empty sums are zero.

source.place: Hironaka (1970), Lemma 18, pp.174–175, including its two particular consequences. Read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED. ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only; no Stacks tag states this assertion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-projective-order-triangular-coordinates]. Permuting the affine variables preserves total degree, the local-power hypothesis, and the requested equation, so use its coordinates. Write $R=k[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e]$, weighted by $\deg\sigma_i=q_i$, and $Y=(X_1,\ldots,X_e)$, $W=(X_{e+1},\ldots,X_r,X_0)$. All $\phi_j$ lie in $R$. Put $I=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_b)R$. Define $E\subset\mathbf N^e$ to consist of the lexicographically largest exponents of nonzero elements of $I$, viewed as polynomials in the algebraically independent $\sigma_i$. The cited node gives the unique expansion $\psi=\sum f_{A\beta}(W)\sigma^AY^\beta$, with $\beta\in\Delta$ and $\deg f_{A\beta}=d-q\cdot A-|\beta|$.

source.place: Agent-written details of Hironaka (1970), (13.2), p.168, and Lemma 18, first paragraph, p.174; read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Reduce this expansion as follows. If a coefficient $f_{A\beta}\ne0$ has $A\in E$, choose $G\in I$ with leading exponent $A$. Take its weighted-degree $q\cdot A$ component and divide by its nonzero leading coefficient. This gives a monic weighted homogeneous $G_A$ with the same leading exponent. From any finite expression in the generators of $I$, taking that degree component gives $G_A=\sum_jQ_{Aj}\phi_j$, with $Q_{Aj}$ of weight $q\cdot A-e_j$ (zero for negative weight). Subtract $f_{A\beta}(W)Y^\beta G_A$ and record its multiples $f_{A\beta}Y^\beta Q_{Aj}$. Each recorded coefficient is homogeneous in $B$ of degree $d-e_j$. Choose the largest offending $A$ first and clear all its finitely many $\beta$ coefficients. Every newly introduced exponent is strictly smaller than $A$, and $q\cdot A+|\beta|\le d$ throughout. There are only finitely many such pairs because all $q_i\ge1$, so this process terminates. It produces $C_j\in B_{d-e_j}$ and $\psi^*=\psi-\sum C_j\phi_j\in B_d$ whose expansion has $f^*_{A\beta}=0$ for every $A\in E$. This is explicit finite polynomial subtraction using the basis of Step 1, not an appeal to a division theorem.

source.place: Agent-written details of Hironaka (1970), Lemma 18, descending lexicographical reduction, p.174; read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Use [lem-trf-projective-order-completed-normal-form] for these triangular coordinates. Put $\theta_j=\delta(\phi_j)$ and $u=\delta(\psi^*)$. The hypothesis still gives $u-\sum a_j\theta_j\in\widehat N^t$, where $a_j=b_j-\delta(C_j)$ and $\widehat N=N\widehat L$. Suppose $u\notin N^t$. Order preservation gives $s=\operatorname{ord}_{\widehat N}u<t$ and $\operatorname{ord}_{\widehat N}(\sum a_j\theta_j)=s$. We can arrange $a_j\in\widehat N^{\max(0,s-e_j)}$ without changing this sum. Indeed let $m=\min_j(\operatorname{ord}_{\widehat N}a_j+e_j)$. If $m<s$, the sum lies in $\widehat N^{m+1}$, and [lem-trf-projective-order-filtered-syzygy-lifting] at $q=m$ gives an exact relation $(v_j)$ with $a_j-v_j\in\widehat N^{\max(0,m+1-e_j)}$. Replace $a_j$ by $a_j-v_j$, increasing the minimum by at least one. At most $s$ repetitions suffice. A zero or empty sum cannot have finite order $s$, so those cases already contradict the supposition. All later computations take place in the completion; no descent of its coefficients is needed.

source.place: Agent-written details of Hironaka (1970), Lemma 18, use of Lemma 17 to bound coefficients, p.174; read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text:
The polynomial expansion of $\psi^*$ dehomogenizes to $\sum f^*_{A\beta}(t_{e+1},\ldots,t_r,1)\rho^At_1^{\beta_1}\cdots t_e^{\beta_e}$. Its coefficient functions belong to $L_0$. Substituting $t_i=z_i+a_i$ and expanding each coefficient in $\widehat L_0=F[[\omega]]$ gives the unique normal expansion $u=\sum g_{A\beta\gamma}\rho^Az^\beta\omega^\gamma$. A binomial expansion only decreases each $\beta_i$, so the bound $\beta_i<q_i$ persists. Neither operation changes $A$, hence $g_{A\beta\gamma}=0$ whenever $A\in E$. By the weighted-order formula the weight-$s$ part $u_{[s]}$ is a nonzero finite sum of these monomials. Write $\phi_j=P_j(\sigma)$ with $P_j$ weighted homogeneous of weight $e_j$. The coefficient comparison of the cited node gives $\theta_j-P_j^{\epsilon_0}(\rho)\in\widehat N^{e_j+1}$. The bounds of Step 3 therefore imply
$$u_{[s]}=\sum_j(a_j)_{[s-e_j]}P_j^{\epsilon_0}(\rho).$$
Here the bracket selects the indicated weighted normal terms, and a negative bracket is zero. To check the equality, subtract the two sides in the actual series: $u-\sum a_j\theta_j$ has order at least $t>s$, while replacing each $\theta_j$ by $P_j^{\epsilon_0}(\rho)$ changes the sum by order at least $s+1$. The normal-order formula forces every remaining weight-$s$ coefficient to vanish. Multiplication by $P_j^{\epsilon_0}(\rho)$ preserves the bounded $z$ exponents, so this comparison uses the unique normal expansion directly.

proof.text:
Leading exponent sets of polynomial ideals are unchanged by a field extension. Here is the needed elementary verification for $k\hookrightarrow F$ via $\epsilon_0$. If $H=\sum_jA_jP_j^{\epsilon_0}$ is a nonzero member of the extended ideal in $F[S]$, take a $k$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_l$ of the finite-dimensional span of all coefficients of the $A_j$. Expanding in that basis writes $H=\sum_
u v_
u H_
u$, with $H_
u\in(P_j)k[S]$. Linear independence makes a coefficient of $H$ zero exactly when every corresponding coefficient of $H_
u$ is zero. Thus the largest exponent of $H$ is the largest of their leading exponents, and belongs to $E$. Conversely every exponent in $E$ survives field extension. Apply this to the identity of Step 4, and collect one fixed pair $( eta,\gamma)$ for which the nonzero $u_{[s]}$ has a nonzero coefficient polynomial in $ho$. That polynomial lies in $(P_j^{\epsilon_0})F[S]$, so its largest exponent is in $E$. But every exponent in it is outside $E$ by Step 4. This contradiction proves $u\in N^t$, and Step 2 supplies the required homogeneous $C_j$.

source.place: Agent-written details of Hironaka (1970), Lemma 18, final leading-exponent contradiction, p.175, including the scalar-extension observation preceding (16.1), p.171; read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For $t=d$, the definition of $U_d$ applied to $\psi^*\in B_d$ gives $\psi^*\in U_d$. For $t>d$, suppose $\psi^*\ne0$. Since $N^t\subseteq N^d$, it is a nonzero member of $U_d$. The singleton family $(\psi^*)$ minimally generates its ideal: the ideal of the other, empty family is zero. Apply [lem-trf-projective-order-initial-minimality] with $b=1$ and degree $d\ge1$. It gives $\operatorname{ord}_N\delta(\psi^*)=d$, contradicting $\delta(\psi^*)\in N^t$ for $t>d$. Therefore $\psi^*=0$ and $\psi=\sum C_j\phi_j$. The argument includes $b=0$, $r=0$, zero $\psi$, and zero coefficients.
